Plasmid cloning
Unless stated otherwise, cloning was performed using the Hieff Clone One Step Cloning Kit (YEASEN). The DNA fragments of AcrIIA1, AcrIIA2, AcrIIA4, AcrIIA5-D1126, AcrIIA5, hA3A, hA3Bctd, hA3Gctd, evoEc48, evoTf1, La, Npu intein, viral nucleocapsid protein, MLH1-SB, and sgRNA scaffolds of SpCas9 were synthesized by GenScript. PCR was performed using Phanta Max Super-Fidelity DNA polymerase (Vazyme). Site-directed mutagenesis of was performed using Mut Express II Fast Mutagenesis Kit V2 (Vazyme).

The DNA fragments of hA3A, hA3Bctd, and hA3Gctd were amplified and cloned into the backbone of pCMV-BE311 (Addgene #73021) to construct CBEs. The DNA fragment of Acrs were amplified and cloned into the backbone of pcDNA3.1(-). The DNA fragments of evoEc48 and evoTf1 were amplified and cloned into the backbone of pCMV-PE219 (Addgene #132775) to construct PE6a and PE6c. The SpRY was cloned from RTW502554 (Plasmid #140003) to construct nSpRY-PE2ΔRNaseH. AAV vectors were constructed based on the backbone of pAAV-EFS-CjCas9-eGFP-HIF1a55 (Plasmid #137929). The sgRNA scaffolds of SpCas9 were cloned into pUC57 under the U6 promoter amplified from the PX459 v2.0 plasmid. Protospacer oligos were phosphorylated by PNK (Thermo Fisher Scientific) and cloned into sgRNA expression plasmids by T4 DNA Ligase (Thermo Fisher Scientific). The pegRNA 3’ extension sequences were added in sgRNA expressing plasmids by PCR. The amino acid sequences or nucleotide sequences were list in Supplementary Data 1 and Supplementary Data 2. All newly generated plasmids used in this study are available from the corresponding author upon reasonable request.

Culture condition and transfection
HEK293T cells (ATCC CRL-3216), HeLa cells (ATCC CCL-2), and U2OS cells (ATCC HTB-96) were kept in Dulbecco’s modified Eagle medium (DMEM, Gibco) supplemented with 10% (vol/vol) fetal bovine serum (FBS, Gibco) in 5% CO2 incubator at 37 °C. HepG2 cells were obtained from Procell Life Science & Technology Co., Ltd. (CL-0103) and were kept in HepG2 cell complete medium (Procell, CM-0103).

Cells were seeded into 48-well plates (Corning) at a density of 55,000 cells per well and transfected 18 h after plating. Transfection was performed using Lipofectamine 3000 (Invitrogen) following the manufacturer’s instructions. For each well, 500 ng of SpCas9, CBE, or PE expression plasmid (9753 bp for PE2), 200 ng of pegRNA or sgRNA expression plasmid (3200 bp), and a variable amount of AcrIIA5 expression plasmid (5869 bp) were co-transfected to achieve the desired molar ratio of AcrIIA5 relative to PE2. At a molar ratio of 0.1, the corresponding mass of AcrIIA5 plasmid is ~30 ng, while at a ratio of 3.0, it is ~900 ng. For PE3 conditions, the nicking sgRNA expression plasmid was also included at 200 ng per well. All plasmid ratios refer to molar amounts unless otherwise specified.

Production and transduction of AAV vectors
AAV vectors were packaged in AAV DJ capsids by OBiO Technology and validated using quantitative PCR. The vector titres were 5.82×1012, 1.02×1013, and 7.36×1012 v. g. /mL for AAV_PE_1, AAV_PE_2, and AAV_AcrIIA5, respectively. After diluting AAV_PE_1 and AAV_PE_2 to 5.00×1010 and 5.00×1010 titres in Opti-MEM I Reduced Serum Medium (Gibco), 10 µL of each was mixed and transduced into HEK293T cells that had been cultured in a 48-well plate to 50% confluence. AAV_AcrIIA5 was diluted to 3.00×1010 first and then serially diluted in 5-fold increments, then 10 μL of each was added to the wells containing HEK293T cells with AAV_PE_1 and AAV_PE_2, either immediately or 12 h later. Besides, an equal volume of medium without AAV_AcrIIA5 was simultaneously added to the control wells containing AAV_PE_1 and AAV_PE_2 for control.

mRNA production and LNP delivery
mRNA of PE2ΔRNaseH and AcrIIA5 were synthesized using the T7 High Yield RNA Synthesis Kit for Co-transcription (Yeasen) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Briefly, plasmids harboring the coding sequence of PE2ΔRNaseH or AcrIIA5 were first constructed with an upstream inactivated T7 promoter, a 5’-untranslated region (UTR), and a Kozak sequence, as well as a downstream 3’-UTR. PCR was used to generate in vitro transcription templates by restoring the functional T7 promoter and appending a 115-nucleotide poly(A) tail downstream of the 3’ UTR. Then, linearized DNA templates containing the T7 promoter were used for in vitro transcription in a 20 µL reaction system, which included T7 RNA polymerase mix, transcription buffer, canonical and modified nucleotides (ATP, CTP, GTP, and N¹-methyl-pseudouridine-UTP), and a cap analog (GAG). The reaction was incubated at 37 °C for 3 h, and the reaction was treated with DNase I to remove the DNA template, and RNA was purified via lithium chloride precipitation. The RNA pellet was washed with cold ethanol, resuspended in RNase-free water, and quantified by UV spectrophotometry. RNA quality and integrity were assessed by agarose gel electrophoresis. Chemically synthesized pegRNAs (GenScript) were modified with 2’-O-methyl and phosphorothioate linkages at the first three and last three nucleotides, and were purified by high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC).

mRNA and pegRNA was formulated into LNPs using the NeoLNP RNA transfection reagent (SDR8006, Scindy) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Briefly, 400 ng mRNA and 200 ng pegRNA complex were diluted with RNA dilution buffer to a final concentration of 40 ng/μL, and an equal volume of NeoLNP working reagent was added. The mixture was gently pipetted and incubated at room temperature for 10 min to allow complex formation. The resulting mRNA-pegRNA-NeoLNP complexes were then diluted in culture medium to a final mRNA concentration of 20 ng/μL and used immediately for cell transfection. Complexes were applied to cells and incubated under standard culture conditions for 72 h prior to downstream analysis.

Extraction of genomic DNA
To extract HEK293T genomic DNA, cells were washed with PBS once and lysed in 100 µL DNA lysis buffer (10 mM Tris-HCl, pH 8.0, 5 mM EDTA, 0.1% SDS, 30 µg mL−1 proteinase K (YEASEN)) at 37 °C for 1 h. After heating at 80 °C for 20 min, the DNA template solution was stored at –80 °C.

Amplicon sequencing
The primers used to amplify the target regions are listed in Supplementary Data 3. 50 µL PCR with presupposed barcodes reactions were purified with TIANquick Maxi Purification Kit (TIANGEN). The PCR products were added with Illumina-compatible adapters and indices. Final amplicon libraries were sequenced with 150 bp paired-end reads on an Illumina MiSeq instrument, and the RAW data were analyzed by the CRISPResso256. The sgRNA-dependent off-target sites were investigated using Cas-OFFinder57. The primers used to amplify the off-target regions are also listed in Supplementary Data 3.

For samples in which the edit was a single base change, samples were aligned to the wild type amplicon in standard batch mode. To calculate editing efficiency, the base change was multiplied by an indel correction factor. Percent base changes came from the output file titled “Nucleotide_percentage_summary_around_sgRNA.txt”. The indel correction factor was obtained by dividing “reads aligned”/“reads aligned all amplicons” values in the output file titled “CRISPResso-Batch_quantification_of_editing_frequency.txt”. To calculate percent indels, “Discarded” was divided by “reads aligned all amplicons” in the same file.

For samples in which the edit was an insertion or deletion, CRISPResso2 was run in HDR batch mode. Percent editing was calculated by dividing the HDR-aligned reads/reads aligned all amplicons. Unintended indels were calculated by adding the “Discarded” reads from the reference-aligned sequences and the “Discarded” reads from the HDR-aligned sequences and then dividing that sum by “reads aligned all amplicons”. All of these values came from the “CRISPResso-Batch_quantification_of_editing_frequency.txt” output file.

All CRISPResso2 parameters are listed in Supplementary Data 4, and the editing efficiencies were listed in Source Data file.

Western blotting assay
Plasmids expressing PE2 or aPE2 (including the pegRNA) were transfected into HEK293T cells cultured in 24-well plates. After 48 h, cells were lysed using X-RIPA UltraMix (X-Blot), and 10 µL of lysate was mixed with 2.5 µL of 5× SDS loading buffer. After boiling, 10 µL of the mixture was loaded onto a 4–15% gradient SDS-PAGE gel. Proteins were separated by electrophoresis and transferred to a PVDF membrane. The membrane was cut at appropriate molecular weights and incubated with primary antibodies: anti-Cas9 (Genscript, A01935, clone 4A1, 1:500) and anti-GAPDH (Proteintech, 60004-1, clone 1E6D9, 1:1000), respectively. After incubation, the membranes were washed with TBST (20 mM Tris-HCl, pH 8.0, 300 mM NaCl, 0.1% Tween-20) for three times and then incubated with HRP-conjugated goat anti-mouse IgG antibody (Proteintech, SA00001-1, 1:4000). After washing with TBST three times, the membranes were finally incubated with ECL substrate and imaged using an Amersham Imager 600.

Protein expressing and purification
The SpCas9 gene was cloned into a pET28a expression vector containing an N-terminal His6-tag. Site-directed mutagenesis was performed using the Mut Express II Fast Mutagenesis Kit V2 (Vazyme) to introduce the D10A and H840A substitutions. The resulting constructs were transformed into E. coli strain BL21(DE3) for protein expression. Bacterial cultures were grown in LB medium at 37 °C to the mid-log phase, then induced with 1 mM isopropyl β-D-1-thiogalactopyranoside (IPTG) and incubated for 12 h at 18 °C. Cells were harvested by centrifugation and resuspended in lysis buffer (20 mM Tris–HCl, pH 7.4; 300 mM NaCl; 20 mM imidazole; 10% glycerol; 5 mM β-mercaptoethanol) supplemented with 1 mM PMSF. Then the cells were disrupted by sonication and the lysate was centrifuged to remove cell debris. The supernatant was bound to Ni-NTA agarose (Genscript), and bound proteins were eluted via a linear gradient of imidazole (0–500 mM). The eluted protein was further purified using size-exclusion chromatography on a Superdex 200 26/60 column (GE Healthcare).

The synthetic AcrIIA5 gene and mutant genes were cloned into a pET28a vector with an N-terminal His6-tag and a maltose-binding protein (MBP) tag. The resulting constructs were transformed into E. coli strain BL21(DE3), and the His6-MBP-AcrIIA5 fusion proteins were expressed and purified following the procedure described above. The His6- and MBP-tags were cleaved using a tobacco etch virus protease (YEASEN). The AcrIIA5 were finally purified on a Superdex 200 26/60 column (GE Healthcare).

sgRNA Preparation and in vitro DNA cleavage assay
Synthetic DNA templates encoding T7 promoter-driven sgRNAs was obtained from Tsingke (5’-GATCACTAATACGACTCACTATAGGC CGCAGTGTTATCACTCAGTTTTAGAGCTAGAAA-3’). In vitro transcription was performed using a T7 RNA polymerase system (Thermo Scientific), followed by RNA extraction using phenol-chloroform and ethanol precipitation. The RNA pellet was resuspended in nuclease-free water and its integrity was confirmed by agarose gel electrophoresis.

For in vitro DNA cleavage assays, SpCas9, SpCas9 nickase, and sgRNA (each at 200 nM) were pre-incubated in NEB Buffer 3.1 at 37 °C for 10 min to assemble the RNP complex. AcrIIA5 was then added at varying concentrations (20–2000 nM) and incubated for an additional 10 min. Subsequently, 10 nM of pUC57 vector was added and the reaction was carried out at 37 °C for 2 h. To terminate the reaction, proteinase K was added and incubated at 37 °C for 15 min. The reaction products were mixed with loading dye and analyzed via 1.5% agarose gel electrophoresis.

PCSK9 editing and Dil-LDL uptake assay
HepG2 cells were seeded in 24-well plates and cultured for 12 h to reach ~60% confluence. Cells were then transfected with LNP-PE or LNP-aPE, as conducted in the “mRNA production and LNP delivery” section. Control group was treated with working buffer. After 84 h, the medium was replaced with 1 mL of fresh medium. 24 h later, 200 µL of the supernatant was collected for ELISA (JONLNBIO, JL19731) measurement of secreted PCSK9. At the same time, cells were incubated with 10 µg/mL Dil-LDL (Yiyuan Biotechnologies, YB-0011) at 37 °C for 4 h. Following incubation, cells were washed twice with PBS, trypsinized, collected into 1.5 mL EP tubes, washed three additional times with PBS, and was finally resuspended in PBS containing 0.5% BSA. For flow cytometry (Sony ID7000), 20,000 gated cells were analyzed using 549 nm excitation and 570 nm emission detection (ID7000 Acquisition and Analysis Software); mean fluorescence intensity (MFI) was used to represent Dil-LDL uptake (FlowJo 10.5.0). The gating strategy is exemplified in Supplementary fig. 10. The remaining cells were centrifuged and lysed with lysis buffer for genomic DNA extraction, PCR amplification, and deep sequencing to determine editing outcomes.

Statistics and reproducibility
The data were collected under randomized conditions. All statistical analyses were performed on three biologically independent experiments using GraphPad Prism 9 (GraphPad Software). The number of sample size was determined according to standard practice in similar studies and supported by previous publications, ensuring the reproducibility and robustness of the results. Error bars represent means ± s.e.m. For comparisons between control and treatments, P values were calculated using a two-tailed Student’s t-test. For comparisons among three groups in “PCSK9 editing and Dil-LDL uptake assay”, one-way ANOVA followed by Tukey’s multiple comparison test was applied. Structural visualization and analysis of AcrIIA5 were performed using PyMOL (The PyMOL Molecular Graphics System, Version 2.4, Schrödinger, LLC).

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
The manuscript by Chen et al. investigates the novel role of the anti-CRISPR protein AcrIIA5 in augmenting the efficiency and precision of prime editing (PE) systems. Prime editing, which facilitates targeted genomic modifications without inducing double-strand breaks, often results in unintended insertions and deletions. This study demonstrates that AcrIIA5 enhances PE activity while concurrently reducing these undesirable indels. The enhancement effect of AcrIIA5 is observed across various PE architectures (PE2 to PE6), different types of genomic edits (substitutions, insertions, deletions), and endogenous loci. Notably, AcrIIA5 does not increase the activity of Cas9 or base editors, suggesting a unique interaction mechanism with the PE system. Furthermore, the enhancement is position-dependent, indicating a specific binding mode between AcrIIA5 and Cas9. These findings underscore the potential application of Acr proteins in CRISPR/Cas systems beyond their traditional inhibitory functions, paving the way for more efficient and precise genome editing technologies.

Major comments:
1. While I appreciate the study and its implications, the claims presented are often based on a single type of experiment that does not directly address the underlying mechanism. I am missing a biochemical and biophysical dissection and proof of the speculated mechanism on what AcrIIA5 does to RuvC that enhances prime editing. For example, is the improvement due to changes in cleavage kinetics or stabilization of the protein fold that makes it particularly amenable to efficient nicking? Additionally, I would like to see a split-function mutation analysis on Cas9 and AcrIIA5 to demonstrate that the effect is driven by their interaction.
2. Since AcrIIA5 has been identified as a potent inhibitor of many Cas9 orthologues (Garcia et al.), I would like the authors to address whether the function of improving prime editing is also true for other Cas9 orthologues.
2. I would like to see a biochemical experiment showing the effect of AcrIIA5 on both nuclease and nickase activity of Cas9.
3. Can you experimentally address why AcrIIA5 has the most significant effect on PE2 and not on the more advanced versions like PE4 and PE5? I am particularly intrigued by the reverse effect observed with PE7.
4. AcrIIA5 impacts PE2 to varying extents across different loci. Often, the effect is absent. Can you please explain the variation between loci? This raises concerns about the technology's applicability in real genome editing scenarios beyond the extensively studied HEK3 and HEK4 loci.
5. A DNA repair profile analysis of indels generated in the presence or absence of AcrIIA5 is required to determine if there is a bias towards MMEJ or NHEJ. Additionally, please clarify the naming of the position of the installed base. This could help determine if the positional effect of AcrIIA5 on base conversion types is related to the prevention of recleavage by Cas9 after editing.
5. I have serious doubts about the AAV experiments – Figure 5c shows only a modest effect after 12 hours. It makes me question whether this approach works effectively at all. Can you demonstrate a better in vivo application? Have you tried LNP delivery?

Minor comments:
1. Why is the improvement in the insertion and deletion of genomic fragments by AcrIIA5 only modest compared to substitutions?
2. The figure presentation could be improved, such as in Figure 1b and others. What is the reason for plotting fold change on the same plots? This is confusing to the reader.
3. In the introduction, the authors state that 'Guided by pegRNA, the PE2 protein binds to one strand of target DNA and nicks the opposite, PAM-containing strand.' This is not correct; the PE2 protein binds to both DNA strands.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
In this manuscript, the authors proposed and provided extensive data demonstrating that low doses of AcrIIA5 can enhance the editing efficiency of Prime Editing. To the best of my knowledge, this is the first study reporting Cas9 inhibitors AcrIIA5 to improve the editing efficiency of genome editing tool-PE, which is novel and interesting. In the field of CRISPR-Cas, Acr was originally discovered as an inhibitor of Cas9, and previous studies have also demonstrated that Acr can inhibit the editing efficiency of Cas9 and BE. Therefore, this study unexpectedly found that Acr can enhance the efficiency of PE, offering new insights for the design and optimization of Acr and PE.

In sum, I find this research to be novel and interesting. The manuscript is well-organized, the methods are sound, the data is detailed and provides strong support for the conclusions. the conclusions are reliable. It will attract widespread interest among researchers in the CRISPR field.

However, I have a few suggestions for the authors.
1. The study focuses on AcrII5 enhancing the efficiency of various PE constructions and reducing indel, but lacks an explanation of the mechanism.
2. The authors compared the editing efficiency of Acr:PEplasmids at different ratios and found that a ratio of 0.1 yielded the best efficiency. However, the Materials and Methods section does not specify the exact amount of Acr plasmid added. I suggest that the authors provide a more detailed protocol to facilitate replication by other researchers. For example, in this study, 500 ng of PE plasmid and 200 ng of pegRNA plasmid were added per well, so does a 0.1 ratio of Acr mean 50 ng? A ratio of 3 would mean 1500 ng? And is the amount of nick gRNA also 200 ng?
3. Could the authors provide Western blot data to demonstrate that the increase in editing efficiency is not due to changes in PE expression levels? At least, could they provide WB data for the 0.1 ratio condition in Fig. 1d?
4. Since the PE system is too large to deliver easily, this is currently a major issue in the field. The authors used three AAVs to deliver the aPE system they developed; however, a three-AAV system is challenging to implement in practical therapeutic applications, and the efficiency increase in Fig. 5C is not significant. The authors should discuss the challenges of AAV delivery for the aPE system and potential solutions.
5. Will the authors submit the plasmids constructed in this study to Addgene to facilitate use by interested researchers?
6. The annotations in the main text does not correspond to the graph in Figure 1e, should correspond to Fig1d?
7. There is no F1i mentioned in the Fig1.
8. The study focuses on AcrII5 enhancing the efficiency of various PE constructions and reducing indel, but lacks an explanation of the mechanism.
9. The study needs more application, such as animal model, to verify the effect of aPE.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
Thank you for the opportunity to review this manuscript entitled “Anti-CRISPR protein AcrIIA5 can enhance the activity and security of prime editing” by Chen, et al.

In this manuscript, the authors describe an approach for improving the efficiency of prime editing in HEK293T cells by co-expressing a phage-derived anti-CRISPR protein, AcrIIA5. In what likely began as an exploration of applying anti-CRISPR proteins to inhibit CRISPR-based gene editing tools, the authors came upon the surprising result that AcrIIA5, an anti-CRISPR protein with established Cas9 inhibitory activity, counterintuitively improved the editing efficiency of prime editing while also decreasing undesired indel byproducts. The effect appeared specific to prime editing and AcrIIA5, as AcrIIA5 inhibited the activity of Cas9 nuclease and base editors, and other anti-CRISPR proteins inhibited prime editing, as expected. The authors optimized the ratio of prime editing and AcrIIA5 components delivered to cells targeting a sentinel site, then characterized the system co-expressing AcrIIA5 with prime editing components (named aPE) on a variety of prime edit types and positions at different genomic loci. The authors found that the efficiency of single base substitution edits at the +1 through +4 positions improved with aPE (that is, substitutions within 4 bp of the PE-induced nick), but that substitution edits at the +5 and +6 position (which are notably the critical G bases of the PAM) decreased in efficiency as evaluated across 4 genomic target sites in HEK293T cells. The authors went on to evaluate aPE with several prime editing formats, prime editor protein variants and edit types, including PE3 (which incorporates a second nicking guide RNA), PE4 (which incorporates an MLH1dn protein for MMR inhibition), PE5 (nicking plus MLH1dn), PE6 variants, SpRY Cas9 variants, insertion edits and deletion edits. Modest improvements to editing efficiency were observed across these edits, except for deletions over 3-bp. The authors then applied aPE to install pathogenic variants in HEK293T cells with modest improvement in efficiency observed over standard PE. Delivery of the aPE system with AAV, however, did not lead to improved editing efficiency compared to a standard PE system, despite attempts to titrate the amount of the AcrIIA5 component. Several attempts were made to understand the origins of the AcrIIA5 improvements, including evaluating pegRNA features like the RTT and PBS length, although none of these revealed a feature influencing aPE activity. Lastly, the authors proposed a mechanistic model for how AcrIIA5 might improve prime editing efficiency.

Major comments
The authors cite prior publications proposing that AcrIIA5 (used in aPE) inhibits Cas9’s RuvC nuclease domain, which prime editing relies upon to nick the non-target DNA strand to generate a primer for initiating reverse transcription. Therefore, it is unexpected that AcrIIA5 would improve prime editing efficiency instead of inhibiting prime editing, particularly when AcrIIA5 inhibits Cas9 nuclease and base editing activity. The observation that AcrIIA5 can improve prime editing is therefore an interesting finding, and potentially a useful one, if it could be properly exploited.

The data presented in the manuscript show that the aPE system can improve prime editing efficiency in HEK293T cells in a somewhat site-dependent manner. In most cases, aPE provided modest benefits in efficiency and product purity. A critical finding is that the aPE system is detrimental when edits are made to the essential G bases of the PAM in the +5 and +6 positions (by either substitution or deletion). It has previously been demonstrated that PAM edits improve prime editing efficiency and decrease undesired indel byproducts, presumably because they prevent re-nicking of the prime-edited strand within the heteroduplex intermediate, which would promote reversion of the intended edit back to the original sequence or indel formation in the context of PE3. Moreover, there is a clear AcrIIA5 dose-dependence of the effect, suggesting it is deleterious to have too much AcrIIA5 and that tuning AcrIIA5 activity is important to achieve the desired outcome. It therefore seems that the simplest explanation for how AcrIIA5 affects prime editing (in a way that is consistent with its known activities) is that it decreases the effective Cas9 nicking activity enough so that re-targeting of the edited strand is slowed, but not so much that the initial necessary nicking activity is too weak. If PAM edits are made that prevent re-nicking on their own, then there is no benefit from AcrIIA5, which can then only weaken the initial nicking activity and decrease the overall editing efficiency. This also potentially explains the site-to-site variability that is observed, as different spacers likely have different intrinsic nickase properties.

With the above in mind, the following additional data and revisions would substantially strengthen the manuscript:
1. To distinguish whether the observed decrease in aPE for +5 and +6 position edits is due to the distal nature of the edit or the edit being part of the PAM, the authors should evaluate more broadly the impact of AcrIIA5 co-expression on prime edits downstream of the PAM (position +7 and beyond), and proximal edits coupled with PAM-silencing edits (e.g., +1 and +5). There are existing pegRNAs reported in the literature that make edits at these positions which could be readily tested.
2. The PE4 and PE5 systems used in this manuscript do not appear to represent the state-of-the-art systems, which co-express MLH1dn proteins separately from the PE protein. The fusion proteins used in this manuscript do not appear to improve prime editing efficiency as would be expected for PE4 and PE5 systems. As the interplay of re-nicking and MMR seem critical to understanding the potential utility of the aPE system, the experiments with PE4 and PE5 should be repeated so that the effects of MLH1dn are consistent with prior publications by separately expressing MLH1dn.
3. The data presented in this manuscript appear to be entirely from HEK293T cells. The efficacy of aPE should be evaluated in several other mammalian cell types to characterize the effects in those contexts.
4. Much of the data presented in the main figures are not essential to supporting the main conclusions of the manuscript (e.g., compatibility with different prime editor proteins in figure 2, the AAV experiment in figure 5, pegRNA features in figure 6). These would be more appropriate as supplementary figures.
5. The mechanistic model appears somewhat speculative and would require further experimental data to support inclusion in this manuscript.

Minor comments
1. Most figures do not indicate the cell type used in the experiment. This information should be added either directly to the figures or to the legend.
2. It appears the same data are presented in figure 1f and supplementary figure 2.
3. In the description of quantitative results, relative editing or indel formation efficiency would be better represented as fold-changes as opposed to % changes, since % change could be interpreted as differences in %. For example, “AcrIIA5 reduced indels by 78.0% (aPE2) and 81.9% (aPE3) for PE2 and PE3, respectively” could be changed to 4.5-fold and 5.5-fold.
4. Abbreviations, like RHA, need to be defined in the text when first used.
5. When using the terminology AAV1, AAV2, and AAV3, there is confusion with serotype, so the naming of these constructs should be changed to avoid this potential confusion.
6. Figures 5b and 5c are challenging to interpret, and the colored shading with inversion of the direction of the bars is not helpful. Recommend reformatting to a standard layout without shading red or green and using clear headers for the graphs conveying that the timepoints indicate when the AcrIIA5 AAV was added.

absent. Can you please explain the variation between loci? This raises concerns
about the technology's applicability in real genome editing scenarios beyond the

Response: Indeed, in our initial investigations, we observed that AcrIIA5 enhances PE
efficiency to varying degrees across different target loci, and in certain cases, it even
appears to reduce PE activity. This variation also prompted us to explore the underlying
factorsthatdeterminethelocus-dependenteffectofAcrIIA5onPEefficiency.
As mentioned above (Fig. 5g in the revised Main text), we hypothesized that aPE
activity may be associated with the initial DNAcleavage activity of Cas9. Specifically, we
proposed that target sites with intrinsically high Cas9 cleavage activity are more likely to
tolerateAcrIIA5-mediatedinhibition,astheystillpermittheinitialnickingeventrequiredfor
initiating PE. In this context, AcrIIA5 may help improve editing efficiency by delaying
re-nicking and reducing unwanted repair events. In contrast, at sites with low inherent
Cas9 cleavage activity, AcrIIA5 may excessively preventing the initial nicking step and
thereby abolishing PE activity. In other words, high Cas9 activity ensures that the
essential nicking still occurs, while AcrIIA5 acts as a brake to prevent excessive or

mistimed cuts that could disrupt the editing process. Under this hypothesis, strong initial
nickingactivitywoulddirectlyresultinhigheraPEefficiencycomparedtothePEsystem.
Hence, we sought to determine whether a correlation exists between Cas9 cleavage
activity and aPE performance. Given that in vitro Cas9 cleavage assays may not
accurately reflect chromatin accessibility and other cellular factors influencing cleavage
efficiencyinvivo,weturnedtoacell-basedpredictiveapproach.WeutilizedDeepSpCas9,
a deep learning model (Kim et al., Sci Adv. 2019; 5: eaax9249.) which predicts SpCas9
cleavage activity across thousands of genomic loci in HEK293T cells. By inputting the
sequences of our tested loci into this model, we obtained predicted cleavage scores
(Supplementary Table 5 in the revised Supplementary Data), where higher scores
indicatestrongerCas9activityincellularcontexts.
By correlating the DeepSpCas9 scores with the observed fold change in editing
efficiency between aPE and PE systems (aPE:PE ratio), we found a strong association:
higher predicted SpCas9 activity scores generally linked to greater enhancement by
AcrIIA5 (Fig. 5h in the revised Main text). Specifically, at target sites with DeepSpCas9
scores above 50, aPE consistently outperformed PE. In contrast, at sites with scores
below50,aPEoftenshowedreducedefficiencycomparedtoPE.
To further validate this observation, we selected an additional set of four loci with
predicted DeepSpCas9 scores >50 and four with scores <50 (Supplementary Table 5 in
the revised Supplementary Data). The results showed that all four high-score loci
exhibited enhanced editing efficiency with aPE compared to PE, whereas all four
low-scorelocishowed reduced aPE activitycompared to PE (Fig. 5i in the revisedMain
text). These findings support the conclusion that the performance of aPE is indeed
influenced by initial Cas9 cleavage activity at the target locus, and that
DeepSpCas9 scores can be prospectively used to guide locus selection, thereby
improving the predictability and applicability of aPE in practical genome editing
scenarios.

predicted cleavage score (69.8) but still showed reduced aPE editing efficiency,
suggestingthatadditionalfactorsinfluenceaPEactivitybeyondinitialcleavageactivity.To
address this, we plan to evaluate aPE editing outcomes at tens of thousands of genomic

investigation will lay the foundation for developing a deep learning model that integrates
both target sequence and pegRNA features, ultimately enabling more accurate and

Based on our newly-obtained experimental results, we attempted to establish a model
toexplainthemechanismoftheaPEsystem(Fig.5gintherevisedMaintext).Previous
studies have demonstrated that PAM-silencing edits can enhance PE activity and reduce
undesiredindelbyproducts,presumablybypreventingre-recognitionandre-nickingofthe
edited strand. (Anzalone et al. Nature 2019;576:149-157). Such re-nicking can lead to
reversion of the desired edit or promote indel formation, especially in the context of PE3
systems. Inspired by these findings, we speculated that the activity of aPE might also be
influenced by a similar prevention of re-nicking mechanism (Fig. 5g in the revised
Main text). Specifically, for PAM-proximal or distal edits, AcrIIA5 may suppress
nSpCas9-H840A nicking activity just enough to slow re-targeting of the edited strand,
without completely abolishing the initial nicking required for initiating the PE process.
Moreover, once the intended mutations are installed, the edited targets may exhibit
reduced binding affinity for the original nSpCas9-H840A-pegRNA complex due to
sequence mismatches within the spacer region, making them more resistant to
re-targeting and potentially further delaying re-nicking in the presence of AcrIIA5. In
contrast, for PAM-silencing edits, the inhibition provided by the PAM mutation itself may
already be sufficient to prevent re-nicking. Thus, the additional suppression fromAcrIIA5
couldoverlyweakentheinitialnickingactivity,therebyreducingtheoverallediting.
Based on this model, we hypothesized that the performance of aPE is closely tied to
the intrinsic DNA cleavage activity of Cas9 at each tested target site. At loci with high
cleavage activity, initial nicking is more likely to occur even in the presence of AcrIIA5,
allowing the PE process to proceed efficiently. In such cases, AcrIIA5 may primarily
function to suppress excessive re-nicking, thereby enhancing editing precision and
efficiency. Conversely, at sites with low Cas9 activity, AcrIIA5 may overly inhibit nicking,
ultimatelyreducingeditingefficiency.

allowing the PE process to proceed efficiently. In such cases, AcrIIA5 may primarily
function to suppress excessive re-nicking, thereby enhancing editing precision and
efficiency. Conversely, at sites with low Cas9 activity, AcrIIA5 may overly inhibit nicking,
