### Reviewer 3

Thank you for the opportunity to review this manuscript entitled “Anti-CRISPR protein AcrIIA5 can enhance the activity and security of prime editing” by Chen, et al.

In this manuscript, the authors describe an approach for improving the efficiency of prime editing in HEK293T cells by co-expressing a phage-derived anti-CRISPR protein, AcrIIA5. In what likely began as an exploration of applying anti-CRISPR proteins to inhibit CRISPR-based gene editing tools, the authors came upon the surprising result that AcrIIA5, an anti-CRISPR protein with established Cas9 inhibitory activity, counterintuitively improved the editing efficiency of prime editing while also decreasing undesired indel byproducts. The effect appeared specific to prime editing and AcrIIA5, as AcrIIA5 inhibited the activity of Cas9 nuclease and base editors, and other anti-CRISPR proteins inhibited prime editing, as expected. The authors optimized the ratio of prime editing and AcrIIA5 components delivered to cells targeting a sentinel site, then characterized the system co-expressing AcrIIA5 with prime editing components (named aPE) on a variety of prime edit types and positions at different genomic loci. The authors found that the efficiency of single base substitution edits at the +1 through +4 positions improved with aPE (that is, substitutions within 4 bp of the PE-induced nick), but that substitution edits at the +5 and +6 position (which are notably the critical G bases of the PAM) decreased in efficiency as evaluated across 4 genomic target sites in HEK293T cells. The authors went on to evaluate aPE with several prime editing formats, prime editor protein variants and edit types, including PE3 (which incorporates a second nicking guide RNA), PE4 (which incorporates an MLH1dn protein for MMR inhibition), PE5 (nicking plus MLH1dn), PE6 variants, SpRY Cas9 variants, insertion edits and deletion edits. Modest improvements to editing efficiency were observed across these edits, except for deletions over 3-bp. The authors then applied aPE to install pathogenic variants in HEK293T cells with modest improvement in efficiency observed over standard PE. Delivery of the aPE system with AAV, however, did not lead to improved editing efficiency compared to a standard PE system, despite attempts to titrate the amount of the AcrIIA5 component. Several attempts were made to understand the origins of the AcrIIA5 improvements, including evaluating pegRNA features like the RTT and PBS length, although none of these revealed a feature influencing aPE activity. Lastly, the authors proposed a mechanistic model for how AcrIIA5 might improve prime editing efficiency.

Major comments
The authors cite prior publications proposing that AcrIIA5 (used in aPE) inhibits Cas9’s RuvC nuclease domain, which prime editing relies upon to nick the non-target DNA strand to generate a primer for initiating reverse transcription. Therefore, it is unexpected that AcrIIA5 would improve prime editing efficiency instead of inhibiting prime editing, particularly when AcrIIA5 inhibits Cas9 nuclease and base editing activity. The observation that AcrIIA5 can improve prime editing is therefore an interesting finding, and potentially a useful one, if it could be properly exploited.

The data presented in the manuscript show that the aPE system can improve prime editing efficiency in HEK293T cells in a somewhat site-dependent manner. In most cases, aPE provided modest benefits in efficiency and product purity. A critical finding is that the aPE system is detrimental when edits are made to the essential G bases of the PAM in the +5 and +6 positions (by either substitution or deletion). It has previously been demonstrated that PAM edits improve prime editing efficiency and decrease undesired indel byproducts, presumably because they prevent re-nicking of the prime-edited strand within the heteroduplex intermediate, which would promote reversion of the intended edit back to the original sequence or indel formation in the context of PE3. Moreover, there is a clear AcrIIA5 dose-dependence of the effect, suggesting it is deleterious to have too much AcrIIA5 and that tuning AcrIIA5 activity is important to achieve the desired outcome. It therefore seems that the simplest explanation for how AcrIIA5 affects prime editing (in a way that is consistent with its known activities) is that it decreases the effective Cas9 nicking activity enough so that re-targeting of the edited strand is slowed, but not so much that the initial necessary nicking activity is too weak. If PAM edits are made that prevent re-nicking on their own, then there is no benefit from AcrIIA5, which can then only weaken the initial nicking activity and decrease the overall editing efficiency. This also potentially explains the site-to-site variability that is observed, as different spacers likely have different intrinsic nickase properties.

With the above in mind, the following additional data and revisions would substantially strengthen the manuscript:
1. To distinguish whether the observed decrease in aPE for +5 and +6 position edits is due to the distal nature of the edit or the edit being part of the PAM, the authors should evaluate more broadly the impact of AcrIIA5 co-expression on prime edits downstream of the PAM (position +7 and beyond), and proximal edits coupled with PAM-silencing edits (e.g., +1 and +5). There are existing pegRNAs reported in the literature that make edits at these positions which could be readily tested.
2. The PE4 and PE5 systems used in this manuscript do not appear to represent the state-of-the-art systems, which co-express MLH1dn proteins separately from the PE protein. The fusion proteins used in this manuscript do not appear to improve prime editing efficiency as would be expected for PE4 and PE5 systems. As the interplay of re-nicking and MMR seem critical to understanding the potential utility of the aPE system, the experiments with PE4 and PE5 should be repeated so that the effects of MLH1dn are consistent with prior publications by separately expressing MLH1dn.
3. The data presented in this manuscript appear to be entirely from HEK293T cells. The efficacy of aPE should be evaluated in several other mammalian cell types to characterize the effects in those contexts.
4. Much of the data presented in the main figures are not essential to supporting the main conclusions of the manuscript (e.g., compatibility with different prime editor proteins in figure 2, the AAV experiment in figure 5, pegRNA features in figure 6). These would be more appropriate as supplementary figures.
5. The mechanistic model appears somewhat speculative and would require further experimental data to support inclusion in this manuscript.

Minor comments
1. Most figures do not indicate the cell type used in the experiment. This information should be added either directly to the figures or to the legend.
2. It appears the same data are presented in figure 1f and supplementary figure 2.
3. In the description of quantitative results, relative editing or indel formation efficiency would be better represented as fold-changes as opposed to % changes, since % change could be interpreted as differences in %. For example, “AcrIIA5 reduced indels by 78.0% (aPE2) and 81.9% (aPE3) for PE2 and PE3, respectively” could be changed to 4.5-fold and 5.5-fold.
4. Abbreviations, like RHA, need to be defined in the text when first used.
5. When using the terminology AAV1, AAV2, and AAV3, there is confusion with serotype, so the naming of these constructs should be changed to avoid this potential confusion.
6. Figures 5b and 5c are challenging to interpret, and the colored shading with inversion of the direction of the bars is not helpful. Recommend reformatting to a standard layout without shading red or green and using clear headers for the graphs conveying that the timepoints indicate when the AcrIIA5 AAV was added.
